check.x: Performs hand hygiene, introduces self to the mother and nurse, and handles the infant gently with minimal disturbance.

kids.x: Identifies increased work of breathing [RR 64, nasal flaring, recession].
Asks for SpO2 and identifies hypoxaemia in room air [SpO2 87%].
Auscultates the chest [widespread crackles and wheeze].

check.x: Assesses circulation and hydration [HR 170, CRT 2 seconds, dry mucous membranes, 2 wet nappies in 24 hours].
Assesses disability and exposure [AVPU alert, temperature 37.8°C] and asks about apnoea.
Elicits history of feeding [about 40% of usual intake], age and risk factors for severe disease.
Starts oxygen by nasal prongs once SpO2 is persistently below 90% in room air, with target SpO2 of 90% or above, by 2 minutes.

kids.x: High flow oxygen at 2 L/kg/min = 12 L/min for 6 kg.
Early senior and PICU involvement if apnoea, exhaustion or rising oxygen need.

check.x: Plans escalation if work of breathing or hypoxaemia worsens on standard oxygen:

kids.x: Nasogastric feeds first if unable to maintain oral hydration.
If nasogastric feeds fail or are unsafe, IV isotonic fluid at 2/3 maintenance = 16 mL/h (maintenance 4 mL/kg/h = 24 mL/h for 6 kg).

check.x: Plans hydration as intake is below the infant's needs:
Avoids salbutamol, adrenaline, corticosteroids, antibiotics, hypertonic saline and routine chest X-ray or blood tests.
Orders continuous SpO2 monitoring while on oxygen, frequent reassessment and nasal suction only if the nose is blocked.
Admits to the paediatric ward and states discharge criteria [SpO2 90% or above in room air, feeding adequately, family confident].
Explains in plain language that bronchiolitis is a viral chest infection, worst around day 3 to 5, with cough lasting up to 3 weeks, and acknowledges the mother's worry.
Explains why antibiotics and Ventolin are not used, and why oxygen and tube or drip feeds are needed.
Gives red flags to report: pauses in breathing, colour change, worsening effort, drowsiness or fewer wet nappies. Checks understanding.

desc: This station involves assessing and managing an infant with bronchiolitis, hypoxaemia and poor feeding in the Emergency Department, then explaining the plan to their parent.
explain:
Oxygen

Bronchiolitis is a viral lower airway infection with mucus plugging and airway oedema. Start oxygen if SpO2 is persistently below 90% in room air, and aim for a target of 90% or above. Do not give oxygen for saturations above this, as it can prolong admission.

Escalation

If hypoxaemia or work of breathing worsens on standard oxygen, consider high flow oxygen at 2 L/kg/min and involve senior or PICU staff early, especially with apnoea or tiring.

Hydration

Fast breathing impairs feeding. Offer nasogastric feeds if oral intake is inadequate. If these fail or are unsafe, give isotonic IV fluid at 2/3 maintenance to avoid hyponatraemia.

What not to do

Bronchodilators, adrenaline, corticosteroids, antibiotics, hypertonic saline and routine X-rays or bloods do not improve outcomes and are not recommended.
focus: Bronchiolitis in an infant with increased work of breathing
guide:
A high-performing candidate recognises hypoxaemia and increased work of breathing early, starts oxygen to a clear target, and plans a hydration strategy with correct fractions and weight-based figures. They avoid ineffective drugs, give a clear escalation plan, and explain the illness to the mother empathically in plain language.

A borderline candidate assesses breathing but delays oxygen or gives no threshold or target, orders salbutamol or antibiotics, or gives vague hydration advice. Their explanation to the mother is rushed or jargon-heavy, with few red flags.
patient:
You are the ED nurse assistant. The infant is 4 months old, 6 kg, born at term, previously well, immunised to date. Day 3 of coryza and cough, today breathing fast and taking about 40% of usual feeds, with 2 wet nappies in 24 hours. No apnoea at home, no sick-contact concerns other than a sibling with a cold. The mother is anxious but cooperative.

Opening observations (room air): HR 170, RR 64, SpO2 87%, temperature 37.8°C, CRT 2 seconds, irritable but alert (AVPU: A). BGL not required unless asked (5.2 mmol/L).

Give when asked or examined: nasal flaring, subcostal and intercostal recession, no grunt, widespread crackles and wheeze, no apnoea witnessed, mildly dry mucous membranes, anterior fontanelle normal. No chest X-ray, bloods or viral swab are needed; state they are not available urgently if requested.

Changes in observations:

  • Oxygen started by 2 minutes: SpO2 rises to 92%, RR 58, HR 160.
  • No oxygen by 3 minutes: SpO2 falls to 84%, RR 70, HR 180, intermittent grunt, tiring.
  • If salbutamol, adrenaline, steroid or antibiotic is ordered: no change in observations.
  • No feeding or fluid plan by 5 minutes: the infant refuses a feed and the nappy is still dry; HR 175.
  • If high flow is requested at 5 minutes: it is being set up; SpO2 stays 91 to 92%.

Mother (from 6 minutes): Ask: "Why can't you give Ventolin or antibiotics?" "Why does a tube or drip need to go in?" "How long will this last?" "When can we go home, and what should I watch for?"
points: Start oxygen when SpO2 is persistently below 90% in room air, and target 90% or above.
Supportive care is the treatment: oxygen, hydration and minimal handling.
Use nasogastric feeds before IV fluids, and give IV fluids at 2/3 maintenance.
Salbutamol, adrenaline, steroids, antibiotics and routine investigations are not recommended.
Escalate early to high flow oxygen and senior or PICU review for apnoea, exhaustion or worsening hypoxaemia.
stem: You are the doctor in the Emergency Department. A 4-month-old infant weighing 6 kg has been brought in by their mother with 3 days of runny nose and cough, and today fast breathing and poor feeding. A nurse is at the bedside. You have 2 minutes reading time, then 8 minutes in the station.
tasks: Assess the infant using an A to E approach, state your findings aloud, and start immediate management (3 minutes).
Outline your ongoing management plan to the examiner, including escalation (3 minutes).
Explain the diagnosis and plan to the mother and answer their questions (2 minutes).
title: Infant with increased work of breathing
